newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW - Mexico TV Azteca aims to remain private.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Mexico TV Azteca aims to remain private.

text.p: Mexico's fast-growing, profitable TV network Television Azteca aims to snatch nearly a third of the $1.2 billion local advertising market from long-ruling monopoly Grupo Televisa next year.
The public won't get a slice of the action though.

Bought from the state in 1993 by a group of wealthy Mexican businessmen, Azteca expects to make $100 million at an operating level this year, but has no plans to go public, company president Ricardo Salinas Pliego told Reuters.
Azteca's shareholders, which include Salinas's own electronics and appliance retailer Grupo Elektra, want to see their $650 million investment "mature" before selling, Salinas said in an interview.
"All the group of investors who are in TV Azteca are seeing it long-term," Salinas said. "We think in three or four years would be the best moment to go public."

To make sure the station stays private, Salinas said Azteca is negotiating with banks who helped fund the privatization to buy back options they hold, which give them the right to around 30 percent of the station's shares.
Earlier this year, one of those banks, GBM-Atlantico, said it expected its fellow institutions to sell their shares to the public by year-end, but Salinas said Azteca preferred to buy them in.
"In the next 30 days, we will have official information on this," he said, declining to offer further details.
Azteca has not published results, but Salinas described the company as "very profitable".
"From the first year, we had profits, we have never lost money. This year we think we could have an operating flow of $100 million," he said.

"It's curious that when we bought the concession we paid 30 percent more that our nearest competitor, $150 million more. All our competitors laughed, made fun of us and said we would go bust very soon. Now the criticism is that...we bought it very cheaply".

Salinas is no relation to former president Carlos Salinas de Gortari, but he does have a business link to a member of Mexico's former first family, Raul Salinas. Raul is now in jail on murder and tax evasion charges.
While he was raising funds for the purchase of TV Azteca, Salinas said he accepted a $30 million loan from Raul.

"For me he was simply another investor, like those we met in the roadshow," Salinas said. "That it looks bad, yes. Unfortunately at this point and looking back, it wasn't a smart decision. But it's a decision taken".
Just 37 when he bought Azteca, Salinas strongly rejected accusations made by some Mexican media -- whom he is suing -- of improprieties in the deal.
"If there had been influence-peddling, I would have had to pay money to receive a benefit, not the reverse," he said.

"(Raul) gave the money to me. I at that time didn't know that this gentleman could be involved in dark matters, I didn't have any motive to suspect. What has happened now is very lamentable. I don't know of it is true or not."

Competitor Televisa and a rival Mexican cable operator, Multivision, are launching Direct-To-Home (DTH) satellite-dish based television services in Mexico this year, but Salinas brushed off any threat from this new medium.

"We think that in these Latin countries, although there is a great furore for pay TV, we think its penetration won't be very great because people won't be able to pay for it," he said. "We think pay TV won't exceed 10 percent of homes".
Meanwhile, Azteca claims its audiences and its advertising revenue are growing.
Salinas said the station's two national channels had captured 40 percent of the Mexican TV audience -- which should quickly boost the 20 percent of TV advertising it expects this year.
"Our target is to capture 30 percent of the (advertising) market" in 1997, he said.
Azteca has spent months in a bitter battle of words with Televisa -- something Salinas said was a result of Televisa's loss of its long-held monopoly on private TV in Mexico.

"Previously advertisers had no choice. All they had to do before was one thing ... go to Televisa, take out their cheque book and pay. Now they have an option -- they can negotiate with us or with them."
